t.4.20.1: Tārā, whose face was like the lord of the stars, saw him struck down upon the ground by the death-dealing arrow loosed from Rāma's bow.
t.4.20.2: Seeing Vālin, who was like an elephant, struck down by the arrow, the beautiful lady approached her husband and embraced him.
t.4.20.3: Tārā, her mind scorched by grief and herself stricken, lamented over the lord of the monkeys, who was like great Indra, lying like a tree torn up by its roots.
t.4.20.5: Rise, O tiger among monkeys, and take to your finest bed, for the best of kings such as you do not lie upon the ground.
t.4.20.4: O you of fearsome valor in battle, O mighty hero, best of leapers, why do you not speak today to me, a wretched woman who has never wronged you?
t.4.20.6: Truly the earth must be exceedingly dear to you, O lord of the earth, for even with your life gone you cling to her with your limbs and forsake me.
t.4.20.7: Clearly, O hero, another delightful city like Kiṣkindhā has been righteously brought into being by you, fashioned on the path to heaven.
t.4.20.8: The pleasures that we enjoyed together with you in the honey-scented forests have now, at your appointed time, been brought to an end by you.
t.4.20.9: Now that you, the leader of the great troop-leaders, have returned to the five elements, I am joyless and without hope, sunk in an ocean of grief.
t.4.20.10: My heart must be very hard indeed: though it burns with grief at seeing you struck down upon the ground, it does not burst today into a thousand pieces.
t.4.20.11: Sugrīva's wife was carried off by you, and he was driven into exile; for that deed of yours against him, this is the fruit you have now obtained, O lord of the monkeys.
t.4.20.12: Out of delusion I was reproached by you, though I was intent on your highest good, I who spoke beneficial words, desiring the welfare of the lord of the monkeys.
t.4.20.13: Surely it is Time, beyond all doubt, that has brought about the end of your life, Time by which you have been forcibly brought, helpless, under the power of Sugrīva.
t.4.20.14: I, a wretched woman, who was formerly nurtured without sorrow, shall now live out a miserable widowhood, burning with grief, like one who has no protector.
t.4.20.15: And my heroic Aṅgada, so tender, fondly cherished and accustomed to comfort, in what condition will he live, now that his paternal uncle is overcome with rage?
t.4.20.16: Son, take a good look at your father, who cherished dharma, for the sight of him, dear child, will be hard for you to obtain hereafter.
t.4.20.18: Indeed, a great deed has been done by Rāma in striking you down, and he has freed himself of his debt in the promise made to Sugrīva.
t.4.20.19: Have your desire fulfilled, Sugrīva; you will regain Rumā. Enjoy the kingdom free from anxiety, for your brother, your enemy, has been struck down.
t.4.20.20: Why do you not speak to me with love as I lament like this? Look at these many excellent wives of yours, O lord of the monkeys.
t.4.20.21: Hearing her lament, those monkey-women all around, stricken with grief, embraced the wretched Aṅgada and wailed aloud.
t.4.20.22: O heroic-armed one adorned with armlets, why do you set out today on a long journey, leaving Aṅgada behind? It is not fitting, O you who hold your son dear, to depart like this, abandoning a son so rich in virtues.
t.4.20.23: O lord of lovely and pleasing attire, what unkindness have I or your son done to you, that today, O hero, you abandon me, your companion, and go to the cruel abode of Yama?
t.4.20.24: O long-armed one, if I have thoughtlessly done anything displeasing to you, forgive me for it, O lord of the monkey race; O hero, I bow my head at your feet.
t.4.20.25: Thus Tārā, of flawless complexion, weeping piteously beside her husband together with the monkey-women, resolved to sit down and fast unto death on the ground where Vālī lay.
t.4.20.17: Comfort your son, and give him your parting message, and, having kissed him on the head, go, for you have set out on a journey far from home.
